title: Slope from Two Points: Why the Formula Works

scenes.title: What does the slope really measure?
body: How fast does y change as x changes?
scenes.narration: A line passes through two comma five and six comma thirteen. What is its slope, and what does that answer actually mean? Here is the idea: slope measures how much the output y changes for a corresponding change in the input x. We are not just plugging coordinates into a formula. We are comparing vertical movement with horizontal movement along the same line.

scenes.title: Why rise is divided by run
scenes.formula: m = change in y / change in x
scenes.narration: From A to B, y rises from five to thirteen, a change of eight. At the same time, x moves from two to six, a change of four. We divide eight by four because we want the vertical change per one unit of horizontal change. That is why slope is rise over run: it converts the total movement into a constant rate.

scenes.title: The mistake that flips the sign
body: Keep the SAME point order upstairs and downstairs.
scenes.narration: Now use the formula. Thirteen minus five over six minus two gives eight over four, so m equals two. This is where students often mix things up: they subtract the y-values in one point order and the x-values in the opposite order. That creates a false negative sign. Pick either point first, but keep that same order in both differences.

scenes.title: What does m = 2 mean?
body: m = 2 means: +1 in x  →  +2 in y
The line has a constant rate of change.
scenes.narration: The answer two is not just a number. It means that for every one unit x increases, y increases by two. Starting at two comma five, one step right gives three comma seven, then four comma nine, then five comma eleven. Notice why the formula works: every pair of points on this straight line gives the same vertical-change-to-horizontal-change ratio.

scenes.title: Quick verification
scenes.narration: Quick check: these points lie on y equals two x plus one. At x equals six, two times six plus one is thirteen, exactly our second point. So remember the idea: slope is a rate of change. Compare the y-change with the matching x-change, keep the subtraction order consistent, and interpret the result as change in y per one unit of x.
